It's the property that makes all that stuff happens. Basically, every object going a certain speed wants to keep going that speed. If you're driving in a car at 60mph and toss a piece of paper in the air, then the paper is still traveling 60mph with the car.

The ELI5 answer: Because the paper was moving to begin with (at 60 mph when you held it up), so it will continue to move in the same fashion (at 60 mph) because the only force acting on it is gravity (which pulls it straight down, not back).

The same goes for the bug. It will hover in place moving at 60 mph because the air it is in is also moving at 60 mph, and the other less fortunate bug which splats into the back of your car's cabin (RIP Steve) because he hasn't had time to be slowed by the unmoving air inside your car. For him, five or six feet is not enough time to start moving with the car. He is still more or less stationary (maybe moving a little because of the air resistance) and not moving at 60 mph with you.

The "I want to give myself a headache tonight" / "I want to think about physics because I'm just that much of a nerd" answer:

Above, I am referring to Newton's First Law of Motion. The First Law has two parts which are actually the same.

1) The first part states that an object at rest (e.g. a piece of paper sitting still on a table) will remain at rest until acted upon by a net external force. Rest means not moving, like a Snorlax using Rest, and "net external" here means a that when you add up all the forces, they have to originate from other objects (not from the object itself) and when added, have some sort of nonzero force component. This nonzero component thing means the forces can't cancel each other out. If I push a piece of paper left with one hand and right with the other both using the same amount of force, the paper isn't going to move. I'm just pressing a piece of paper like an idiot.

2) The second part states that an object in motion (e.g. a piece of paper held in a car moving at 60 mph) will remain in motion in a straight line and at constant velocity (redundant I know because vectors blah blah blah) until acted upon by a net external force. Your paper is being acted upon by a net force, but that net force is gravity down minus air resistance up. The resultant is a small downward force which causes the paper to float into your lap. There is no horizontal component of force on the paper. It won't change its horizontal motion because there's nothing to make that change. It will just keep going at 60 mph. If the paper were to fly back into your face or rear window (suddenly, Alfred Hitchcock!), that would actually be as weird, freaky, and ghosty-ish as if a piece of paper on a table suddenly decided to slide to the left. (Slide to the right. Cha cha now y'all.) The flies are then self-explanatory. Fly #1 just sits there peacefully because his air (surroundings) are zooping along at 60 mph. Fly #2 dies a horrible death because he was outside and coming inside is like being hit by a train. The reasoning here should actually probably invoke impulse (momentum change based on force times time) and/or work (energy change based on force times distance) but I'm too tired to write that.
